fileName: 36 - Why Price Might Reverse in Non-Obvious Levels.mkv
displayTitle: Why Price Might Reverse in Non-Obvious Levels

content.fullText: In this lesson, instead of demonstrating the price action reading framework once again, I want to focus on a particular detail about price action, which is the idea that price sometimes reverses in non-obvious places of the price chart. So I'm going to show you one of the possible ways of uncovering these price levels in alignment to the knowledge of intrinsic properties in order to validate these levels. In this chart you can see price action retracing against a downward price vector, so it's natural to look for levels in this downward price vector where the current price action might find difficulty advancing. Notice also that price just created a DFB to the downside. The DFB, of course, is an alert that price might reverse to the downside. The issue here is that the current price action is still far away from the last DFB line or the absolute high as you can see here, which would be the more obvious places where sellers could appear again. Notice how price action is stopping in the same level where there was a contraction in volatility followed by an explosion of volatility to the downside. It's even possible to spot a frequency line in the candlesticks where volatility contracted. This contraction in volatility translates into more price activity in a narrow price range. Another good way of visualizing that is through the use of the volume profile tool, which you can see here. There are three major peaks of volume activity in this downward price vector. This is the last one in the way of price reaching the last DFB line. Notice how the volume profile increases when the downward progressions in terms of range dynamics start to move less prominently to the downside, meaning that price is oscillating up and down more within a narrow price range. This naturally creates a barrier for price because traders act as if these highly traded levels will work as support or resistance levels. Notice that in the second highest peak, price didn't have any trouble getting past it, but it did return to it and reacted as if this level was important. Plotting a pitchfork in the more recent highs and lows, we can see nice intersections between the peaks of the volume profile tool and the outer lines of the pitchfork. The bottom line here is that price will reverse significantly in places of the chart where a lot of different techniques will intersect. So the difficulty of trading can be summed up to the difficulty in finding these intersections, at least from a technical point of view. Finding areas where price might have trouble is not enough. These areas have to coincide with multiple signals that agree with each other. Even when that happens, it's not a guarantee that price will reverse because there are many other forces in the market beyond traders using technical analysis. Nonetheless, this is the best that can be done by a trader using technical analysis. The way to validate if price is going to reverse and enter a self-reinforcing cycle, or just create a small bump, is to look at the intrinsic properties of the candlesticks that react to the level in question. Notice that as price action approaches the level of the third peak in the volume profile tool, we can see a reduction in the body percentage of candlesticks, and that is an indication of uncertainty. We can also see that an upward progression is immediately followed by a downward progression, a bias change, a dynamic frequency breakout, and an increase in the body percentage once again, but now for the downside. In other words, these candlesticks are telling a story about how price is encountering resistance at the third peak of the volume histogram and how strong sellers are entering the scene. If you miss these details, you might have just waited for price to reach the more obvious last DFB line on the top of the chart or the absolute high and then see how price reacts. In this next chart, you can see how price ends up reversing at the level of the third peak in the volume profile tool, and it never had the chance of reaching the last DFB line. If price action only reversed at DFBs or clear tops or bottoms, trading would be extremely easy. The difficulty emerges partly because price might reverse before, and then the trader needs to risk entering a more dangerous position. In this next chart, you can see how price goes down from that point and never tests the more obvious levels.

keyEvents.description: A candlestick chart is displayed, showing a significant downtrend (red candles) followed by a sharp upward retracement (green candles).

Two horizontal black lines are drawn on the chart. The upper line marks the absolute high of the prior downtrend. The lower line marks the high of the current retracement candle, which has a long upper wick, indicating a rejection of higher prices.

A third horizontal black line is drawn. It originates from a point within the previous downtrend characterized by a consolidation (contraction in volatility) right before a large downward move (explosion of volatility). This line coincides with the current price rejection level.

A 'Volume Profile' tool is applied to the prior downtrend, appearing as a horizontal histogram on the left side of the chart. A prominent high-volume node (a peak in the histogram) aligns with the horizontal line drawn at 01:09, where price is currently stalling. A red line is drawn over this peak for emphasis.

A second red horizontal line is drawn to highlight another, lower high-volume node on the volume profile. The price is shown to have moved through this level but later returned to it, treating it as support before continuing upward.

An Andrews' Pitchfork is drawn on the current upward retracement. The upper parallel line of the pitchfork intersects precisely with the upper red line (the high-volume node where price is stalling), creating a point of technical confluence.

The chart animates forward, revealing that the price reversed decisively at the intersection of the pitchfork's upper line and the high-volume node. The price then breaks the upward structure and begins a new, strong downtrend.

semanticAnalysis.mainConcept: The core concept is that significant price reversals often happen at 'non-obvious' levels, which can be identified by finding a confluence of multiple, independent technical analysis techniques. The lesson demonstrates this by intersecting a high-volume node from a Volume Profile (representing a past area of high trading activity and price agreement) with the dynamic boundary of an Andrews' Pitchfork. The final validation comes from analyzing the 'intrinsic properties' of the candlesticks at this intersection, such as a reduction in body size (uncertainty) followed by a 'bias change' and strong momentum in the reversal direction, which confirms the shift in market control.
semanticAnalysis.deeperMeaning: Effective trading analysis requires moving beyond simple support/resistance levels (like swing highs/lows) to understand the market's deeper structure. The market has memory; areas of past consolidation and high volume act as future barriers. The true difficulty and skill in trading lies in identifying these 'intersections' where different analytical models agree, as this significantly increases the probability of a forecast. A trader's job is not just to find these levels but to validate them in real-time by reading the story told by the candlesticks, which reveal the immediate struggle between buyers and sellers.
semanticAnalysis.educationalGoal: The educational objective is to teach traders a sophisticated methodology for locating high-probability reversal points that are not immediately apparent on a price chart. It aims to develop a multi-layered analytical process by integrating volume analysis, geometric tools, and nuanced candlestick interpretation. This lesson fits into a curriculum focused on advanced price action reading, showing how to build a robust, evidence-based trading hypothesis by finding confluence among different technical signals, thereby moving beyond simplistic or single-indicator strategies.
